page: OVHcloud d2-8 is an entry-level virtual machine within the Discovery series, powered by the KVM hypervisor. The instance is configured with 4 shared vCPUs mapped to 4 physical cores on an x86_64 Intel Haswell-era processor clocked at 2.0 GHz. Memory capacity is fixed at 8.0 GB, establishing a 1:2 vCPU-to-memory allocation of 2.0 GB per core. The host CPU features 32 KB of L1 data cache, 4 MB of L2 cache, and 16 MB of shared L3 cache, supporting instruction set extensions including AVX, AES, BMI2, and FMA. Modern vector additions like AVX-512 and AMX are absent, and hardware accelerators such as dedicated GPUs are not present.

Storage consists of a bundled 50 GB local NVMe SSD, providing low-latency solid-state disk access without external network block attachment. The baseline network bandwidth is designated at 0 Gbps, and no complimentary public IPv4 addresses are assigned directly to the instance, which places constraints on public ingress and high-throughput external networking.

Benchmark measurements across processing, cache, and memory access reflect the legacy nature of the shared Haswell architecture. Single-core processing rates low in stress-ng at 917.98 and in Geekbench single-core at 610.0, placing it within the bottom 10% of tested environments. Multi-core performance reaches 3730.94 in stress-ng and 1751.0 in Geekbench. PassMark results similarly mirror this tier, yielding a CPU score of 3428.15 and a memory score of 1125.99. Memory bandwidth reaches 35.67 GB/sec for large uncached reads and 23.03 GB/sec for writes. Database operations in PassMark reached 1717.83, while Redis SET operations yielded 3.03 million operations per second, and static web serving throughput reached 2.96 GB/sec.

From an efficiency standpoint, the d2-8 offers an accessible resource footprint suited for low-cost testing, staging, lightweight internal tooling, and microservices where compute density or execution velocity is not critical. Primary tradeoffs center on the shared legacy compute cores, modest memory allocation, lack of complimentary IPv4 networking, and overall low performance ceiling, precluding it from compute-intensive batch processing or high-throughput production infrastructure.
